poster.title: Day of the Heroic Guerrilla
poster.creator: Elena Serrano
poster.edition: OSPAAAL offset lithograph, 1968, commemorating 8 October; MoMA 503.1987.
poster.alt: A red and white Che Guevara portrait repeats within nested rectangular fields and overlapping maps of Latin America in blue, pink, red and grey.
poster.blurb: A repeated portrait and expanding geographic forms turn a memorial image into a statement of international solidarity.

notes.title: A face repeats outward
notes.body: The central portrait is echoed at larger scales. Repetition makes the figure appear to reverberate across the sheet rather than remain a single isolated likeness.

notes.title: Portrait and territory overlap
notes.body: The outlines of Latin America occupy the same visual space as the face. The composition proposes a relationship between one revolutionary figure and a continental cause.

notes.title: An international address
notes.body: The small heading appears in several languages, while OSPAAAL’s mark sits below. Those details identify the poster’s intended circulation beyond a single national audience.

studyData.intro: A portrait repeats across nested rectangles and an overlapping continental outline. Read the image’s visual argument about an individual and a larger cause, while keeping the poster’s commemorative language distinct from a neutral account of history.

regions.label: The central portrait
regions.summary: The smallest clear face holds the centre.

sections.heading: A face in two strong tones
sections.body: At the centre, a red-and-pale portrait uses sharply bounded shapes rather than smooth modelling. Dark red areas define hair, brow, nose and clothing, while pale gaps supply highlights. The smaller central face is clearer than many of its larger, partially interrupted repetitions.

sections.heading: A named political image
sections.body: The V&A identifies Serrano’s 1968 design as an image connected with Che Guevara and the spread of revolutionary solidarity. This supplies historical identification. The poster presents a supportive political image; studying its form does not require accepting its commemorative judgement as neutral fact.

regions.question: Why is the smallest complete face easier to read than its larger echoes?

regions.label: The portrait’s eyes
regions.summary: A few dark marks establish a gaze.

sections.heading: Direction from minimal detail
sections.body: The eyes and brows are formed by compact red marks within a pale forehead and cheek area. There is little continuous shading. Their arrangement still gives the face a directional gaze, showing how a recognisable portrait can survive a severe reduction in tonal detail.

sections.heading: Looking beyond the frame
sections.body: The gaze can be read as directed beyond the immediate viewer rather than as a frontal encounter. Such a reading may contribute to a sense of resolve, but that is an interpretation of the image. It is not evidence of the subject’s actual thoughts.

regions.question: Which tiny mark most affects the direction of the gaze?

regions.label: The small beret star
regions.summary: A pale symbol punctuates the headwear.

sections.heading: A small repeated accent
sections.body: A pale star sits on the central headwear, with larger echoes appearing above it in the repeated portraits. It is tiny within each face but gains visibility through repetition. The mark connects the central image with the successive enlargements around it.

sections.heading: Symbol and likeness together
sections.body: The star provides a symbolic identifier within a recognisable portrait. Its repeated placement can make the political image feel consistent as it changes scale. This does not mean every star in another poster has the same meaning; the surrounding subject and historical context matter.

regions.question: How does repetition make this very small mark easier to notice?

regions.label: The enlarging faces
regions.summary: A single portrait becomes several scales.

sections.heading: Repetition with interruption
sections.body: The portrait reappears in larger versions around the central image, but rectangular boundaries and overlapping colours interrupt them. Hair, shoulders and headwear can be traced across different bands. The viewer reconstructs repeated forms rather than seeing a row of complete, separate portraits.

sections.heading: Expansion as a visual claim
sections.body: Increasing scale can suggest an image or idea spreading outward. Here that reading is reinforced by the continental shape. The relationship is an argument made by the composition, not a measured map of actual political influence or a factual record of support in each place.

regions.question: Which repeated feature helps you recognise a larger face when most of it is interrupted?

regions.label: The nested rectangles
regions.summary: Repeated borders pull inward and outward.

sections.heading: A sequence of straight edges
sections.body: Several rectangular fields sit inside one another, with blue, pink, grey and dark bands. Their straight edges cut across the softer outlines of hair and geography. The sequence can be followed inward towards the central face or outward towards the limits of the sheet.

sections.heading: Two possible directions
sections.body: Starting at the centre makes the image appear to expand; starting at the outer border makes it seem to concentrate. Both readings are available in the same still arrangement. Try each deliberately before deciding whether the poster feels more like a broadcast or a focal point.

regions.question: Can you make your eye travel outward, then reverse the route?

regions.label: The continental outline
regions.summary: A geographic shape overlaps the faces.

sections.heading: A long irregular silhouette
sections.body: An outline resembling Latin America extends from the upper-left area through the centre and down towards the bottom. It crosses the nested rectangles instead of occupying a separate map panel. Pink and red portions remain recognisable even where portrait and background colours intersect it.

sections.heading: Person and territory compared
sections.body: Putting a portrait and a continental outline in the same space proposes a relationship between a person and a wider political cause. It is not a map of borders, membership or public opinion. The image makes a symbolic comparison that viewers can examine and question.

regions.question: Where does the map remain clearest despite the overlapping portrait?

regions.label: The long southern taper
regions.summary: A narrow shape extends below the face.

sections.heading: A downward continuation
sections.body: The continental silhouette narrows into a long taper below the central portrait. Its pink and red areas cross several horizontal bands. This extension prevents the geographic motif from being confined to the face and carries it towards the lower field of the poster.

sections.heading: A counter-direction to the frames
sections.body: The rectangles suggest expansion around a centre, while the taper gives a strong downward direction. That contrast makes the composition more complex than a simple target. Follow only the taper, then compare the experience of following the nested frames.

regions.question: Which route feels more direct: the downward taper or the surrounding rectangles?

regions.label: The multilingual heading
regions.summary: Several languages name the same commemoration.

sections.heading: An explicitly commemorative phrase
sections.body: The heading repeats the event wording in Spanish, French, English and Arabic. The English line names the Day of the Heroic Guerrilla and October 8. “Heroic” belongs to the poster’s commemorative language; it is a political evaluation printed on the sheet, not a neutral description supplied by this study.

sections.heading: An international communication practice
sections.body: The V&A explains that OSPAAAL commonly used Spanish, English, French and Arabic, and distributed removable posters through Tricontinental magazine. That documents a wider communication practice relevant to the heading. It does not prove the exact journey taken by this particular surviving sheet.

regions.question: How does repeating the message in several languages change the poster’s address?

regions.label: The OSPAAAL mark
regions.summary: A small organisation mark closes the sheet.

sections.heading: A signature of publication
sections.body: A small pale emblem and the letters OSPAAAL appear near the bottom-right corner. They occupy little space compared with the portrait but identify an organisational presence. Their fine lines contrast with the large, flat colour areas that dominate the composition.

sections.heading: A checked production record
sections.body: MoMA attributes this 1968 poster to Elena Serrano and lists OSPAAAL as its printer, with offset lithography as the medium. These are object-record facts. The apparent flatness of the image alone would not be enough to establish that printing process.

regions.question: What information does the small mark add that the portrait cannot provide?

regions.label: The outer blue field
regions.summary: The sheet holds its expanding image within an edge.

sections.heading: A border beyond the frames
sections.body: Blue and dark areas continue around the nested composition, bounded by a narrow outer edge. The top and bottom retain fragments of the enlarging image rather than becoming empty margins. This makes the central construction feel part of a field that reaches the sheet’s limits.

sections.heading: Creases are not graphic arrows
sections.body: Fine fold-like lines and surface variations are visible in the reproduction. They should be distinguished from the deliberately coloured rectangular boundaries. A surviving printed object can carry handling traces; those traces do not automatically express the designer’s intended geometry.

regions.question: Which lines belong to the colour composition, and which look like marks on the surviving sheet?

sources.title: V&A: Solidarity and design—an introduction to OSPAAAL
sources.summary: Identifies the Guevara image and explains OSPAAAL’s multilingual headings and magazine-poster distribution. These are contextual facts, not proof of a specific copy’s circulation.

connections.text: The repeated rectangles become progressively smaller around the central red-and-cream portrait.

connections.text: The continental silhouette travels across the rectangular image, linking a geographic shape to the face at the centre.
